summary: Updates the Digest authentication scheme in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) from RFC 3261 to support stronger hash algorithms such as SHA-256 and SHA-512/256, replacing the obsolete MD5.

eli5.summary: Phone calls over the internet check passwords with a scrambling recipe. The old recipe was weak, so this adds stronger ones.

subtitle: SIP Digest authentication gets stronger hash algorithms such as SHA-256 so MD5 is no longer the only option.

tldr.problem: SIP's Digest authentication, inherited from HTTP, defaulted to the MD5 hash, which is not collision resistant and is now considered a bad choice.
tldr.mechanism: SIP now allows any algorithm in the HTTP Digest hash algorithm IANA registry, adds rules for offering several challenges in order of preference, makes qop mandatory in practice, and clarifies forking and the digest format.
tldr.outcome: SIP servers and clients can use SHA-256 and SHA-512/256. MD5 stays only for backward compatibility and is NOT RECOMMENDED, which leaves a downgrade attack risk.

today: RFC 8760 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2020 that updates RFC 3261. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why SIP Digest Needed an Update
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) in RFC 3261 authenticates users with the same mechanism as HTTP, called Digest Access Authentication. It is a simple challenge-response scheme: a server challenges a request and the client answers with authentication information. RFC 3261 points to RFC 2617 for it.

The default hash is MD5, which has been shown not to be collision resistant (see RFC 6151). RFC 7616 obsoleted RFC 2617, added stronger algorithms, and created the IANA registry named "Hash Algorithms for HTTP Digest Authentication". RFC 8760 updates RFC 3261 so SIP supports the algorithms in that registry.
sections.eli5: SIP checks passwords with a scrambling recipe called MD5. Clever people found the recipe can be fooled, so this RFC lets SIP use better recipes.

sections.title: Hash Algorithms
sections.content:
Digest has an algorithm parameter that names the hash used to compute the response. RFC 3261 specified only MD5, used by default. This document extends it so any algorithm in the IANA registry may be used, and it adds support for SHA-256 and SHA-512/256.

A server (UAS) picks which algorithm to use according to its own policy, in a way that parallels the process in HTTP from RFC 7616.
sections.eli5: The password check can now use a newer, tougher scrambling recipe instead of only the old weak one.

sections.title: Representing Digest Values
sections.content:
The size of a digest depends on the algorithm. Its bits are converted four at a time into lowercase hexadecimal characters from 0123456789abcdef. With SHA-256 or SHA-512/256, the digest is represented as 64 hexadecimal characters.

The ABNF is extended so request-digest can have different sizes: LDQUOT *LHEX RDQUOT. The number of hex digits follows from the algorithm, with a minimum of 32. An empty value is allowed when the client has not yet received a challenge.
sections.eli5: The scrambled result is written out using the digits 0 to 9 and the letters a to f. A bigger scramble makes a longer string.

sections.title: How Servers and Clients Choose a Challenge
sections.content:
When a server (UAS) gets a request without an acceptable Authorization header, it can reply 401 or 407 with a WWW-Authenticate or Proxy-Authenticate header. It MAY add several such headers so it can use the best algorithm the client supports. Headers with the same realm MUST each use a different algorithm, and the server MUST list them from most to least preferred. It cannot assume the client used the top one.

A client (UAC) that receives several challenges for the same realm SHOULD use the topmost one it supports unless local policy says otherwise, and MUST ignore any challenge it does not understand. With a 401 containing different realms, it SHOULD retry with credentials matching the topmost header of any of the realms. If it cannot answer any challenge, it SHOULD give up, unless local policy suggests something such as a non-Digest mechanism.
sections.eli5: A server can offer a menu of password checks, best first. The client picks the first one it understands, and if it understands none it stops trying.

sections.title: Forking Proxies
sections.content:
When a request is forked, several proxies and user agents may each want to challenge the client. The forking proxy is responsible for combining these into a single response, and every WWW-Authenticate and Proxy-Authenticate value received MUST be placed into that response.

When it merges headers from one downstream proxy, it MUST keep their order. The order of values from different downstream proxies is not significant.
sections.eli5: If one call is sent to many places and each asks for a password, the middle helper collects all the questions into one list, keeping each place's own order.

sections.title: Changes to Digest Rules for SIP
sections.content:
SIP clients and servers MUST NOT accept or request Basic authentication. Digest follows the HTTP rules with "HTTP/1.1" replaced by "SIP/2.0" plus several differences. The uri parameter of the Authorization header MUST be in quotation marks, the HTTP example of choosing a nonce from an ETag does not work for SIP, and the HTTP caching text from RFC 7234 does not apply.

Because forwarding by a proxy can make the request-line URI and the Authorization URI refer to different users, a server MUST check that the Request-URI in the header corresponds to a user for whom it will accept forwarded or direct requests, though it MAY still accept it if the two fields differ.

Two semantic changes matter most. First, when a message has no body, the hash of the entity-body is the hash of an empty string; for SHA-256 that is e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855. Second, qop handling is tightened: a server MUST always send qop in its challenges and a client MUST send it in its answer. Receivers must handle it correctly, though for backward compatibility it stays optional to receive from RFC 3261 implementations, with a default of auth. The Authentication-Info header remains allowed because it provides integrity checks over bodies and mutual authentication.
sections.eli5: A few rules are adjusted so the password check works for phone calls: no plain passwords, a clear rule for calls with no message body, and a required extra setting that makes the check safer.

sections.title: ABNF Updates
sections.content: The SIP grammar changes in two places. request-digest becomes LDQUOT *LHEX RDQUOT so digests can be longer than MD5's. The algorithm parameter accepts MD5, MD5-sess, SHA-256, SHA-256-sess, SHA-512-256, SHA-512-256-sess, or any other token, which lets registry algorithms be used.
sections.eli5: The rule book that says how messages are written now allows the new recipe names and longer scrambled results.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This specification adds new secure algorithms for Digest. MD5 remains only for backward compatibility with RFC 2617, and its use is NOT RECOMMENDED.

Keeping MD5 opens the door to a downgrade attack by an on-path attacker. The most effective answers are to validate the client and challenge it accordingly, or to drop backward compatibility by not supporting MD5. Section 5 of RFC 7616 has a detailed security discussion of Digest. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: If the old weak recipe is still allowed, a sneaky person in the middle could try to trick both sides into using it. The best fix is to stop allowing the old recipe at all.
